1.pericope_label: O that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother!... I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please

schools.summary: Delitzsch states the fact the allegory must work around, that Solomon is not the woman's brother, and reads the wish as a dream carrying her into the reality she wanted, with a note on the Hebrew particle meaning in the manner of rather than as though; he also marks the seam, the sixth act opening with the question that opened the third, and reports that the Greek translator, faced with illegible consonants, produced clothed in white. Ellicott reads the whole as a recollection of feelings held before the obstacles to the union were removed, and cites the marginal rendering in which her family would not then have reproached her.

Gill takes the wish for the church's request that Christ stand toward her as a brother, notes that several Jewish writers grant the King Messiah is meant and that many of the ancients read it as the old church's longing for the incarnation, and makes the mother's house the church of the firstborn.

Clarke keeps the scene domestic: the bride fears her fondness will look like excessive familiarity and wishes her lover were a small brother she might kiss in the street; he explains the spiced wine as a strong drink shared from one cup by bride and bridegroom on the wedding day, and marks the end of the sixth night of the marriage week at the fourth verse. Wesley reduces the wish to a desire for stricter union and reads the drink as gifts and graces employed in Christ's service.

Henry has the spouse betrothed but not yet married, the nuptials reserved for the second coming, and therefore obliged to keep a distance; he allows the older reading that this is the Old Testament saints' prayer for a hastened incarnation but prefers to make it every believer's wish for closer communion.

debates.question: What kind of wish is the opening verse?

positions.view: The church's request that Christ act toward her as a brother, which many of the ancients read as a longing for the incarnation.
A betrothed spouse's wish for the innocent freedom of a sister, since the marriage itself waits for the second coming.
A bride's wish that her lover were a small brother, so that she might kiss him publicly without offence.
A recollection of what she felt before the obstacles were cleared, when she could not avow her love openly.
A dream carrying her into the reality she wished for, so that she has in him what a brother is to a sister.

outliers.note: Reads the book as a wedding-week drama and marks the close of the sixth night at the fourth verse.

Marks a structural seam instead, the sixth act opening with the same question that opened the third, where the earlier closed an account of love still growing and this one closes an account of love consummated.

themes: O that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised.
I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother’s house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate.
His left hand should be under my head, and his right hand should embrace me.
I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.

5.pericope_label: Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved?... if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats the seal as a signet-ring worn on a cord at the breast or on the hand, and reads the request as the woman's answer to her husband's recollection of how their love began; Ellicott supplies the section's lexical work — jealousy as ardent passion from a root meaning to be red with flame, the coals as a word used elsewhere of thunderbolts and fever-heat, the closing phrase as literally a flame of Jah, the only divine name in the book — and states his method, that the dramatic theory meets insuperable difficulties here and the theatre must be imaginary.

Gill gives the wilderness question to the daughters of Jerusalem, makes the wilderness the world out of which the church is called, refers the seal to the high priest bearing the tribes' names over heart and shoulders, and concedes that a believer's love may be left but not lost.

Clarke offers two renderings of the obscure clause about the apple tree, reports from his own travels the practice of pricking figures into the skin and staining them with a blue powder that lasts for life, and turns the seventh verse into counsel that pure love cannot be bought; Wesley alone gives the opening question to the bridegroom, defending it by the Hebrew habit of speaking of oneself in the third person.

Henry reads the ascent from the wilderness as conversion and consolation, a sinful state being remote from communion with God and barren of true comfort, and has angels in heaven and friends on earth alike as joyful spectators of the soul that comes up leaning on Christ.

debates.question: Who asks who this is coming up from the wilderness?

positions.view: The daughters of Jerusalem, who have just been charged and now look on with admiration.
The bridegroom, who puts the question in order to answer it himself, speaking of himself in the third person as Hebrew allows.
A signet-ring, carried on a cord at the breast or worn on the hand.
The high priest's engraved stones, or a lover's name or portrait worn on the arm — not a signet worn there.
A tattoo of the kind still pricked into the arms and breast in the Levant and stained with an indelible blue powder.
An engraved tablet worn at the breast, with a signet on the hand.
A symbol of what is especially dear and precious, without further specification.

outliers.note: Points out that the closing phrase of the sixth verse is literally a flame of Jah, the only place in the whole book where a divine name occurs, and takes it adverbially for something superlatively strong.

Draws his explanation of the seal from what he has himself seen in the Levant, where figures are pricked into the skin of the arms and breast and rubbed with a blue powder that lodges under the surface and remains distinct for life.

themes: Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? I raised thee up under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth: there she brought thee forth that bare thee.
Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.

8.pericope_label: We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts: what shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for?... thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred

schools.summary: Ellicott concedes at the outset that commentators are almost unanimous in feeling the poem properly ends at the seventh verse, and that a dramatic construction can find no place for what follows except as a meaningless epilogue; his own account of the book as unordered reminiscences dissolves the difficulty. He makes the wall and door emblems of chastity and its opposite and reads the vineyard as a repudiation of a polygamous establishment. Delitzsch supplies the social background, that brothers are a sister's nearest guardians and precede even father and mother in the matter of marriage, and reads the vineyard speech as a request made to her royal husband.

Gill takes the little sister for the Gentile church as the Jewish church sees her, notes that she says we and not I because the sister belongs to Christ as well, and reads the vineyard as the church under the new dispensation.

Clarke keeps the sister a girl of the bride's household who is not yet marriageable, reports Calmet on the undefended state of an unmarried woman and on the vineyard speech as a refusal of both the vineyard and its profits; Wesley locates Baal-hamon near Jerusalem and makes Christ's title to his vineyard the better, since it was bought with blood and not with money.

Henry frames the whole passage as a married couple consulting about their affairs, yoke-fellows who having laid their hearts together now lay their heads together, and reads the little sister as the Gentile world, little because undignified by the knowledge of God and without breasts because without revelation, scriptures or ministry.

debates.question: Does the poem properly continue past the seventh verse?

positions.view: On a dramatic reading it cannot; commentators are almost unanimous that the poem ends there, and many reject what follows as a later addition. Only an unordered succession of reminiscences leaves this section in place.
It continues without difficulty as a scene at the woman's parental home.
It continues as a consultation between Christ and his church about a sister and a vineyard.

debates.question: What is the vineyard speech doing?

positions.view: Repudiating polygamy: let Solomon keep his harem of mercenary beauties, whose upkeep the two hundred paid to keepers is meant to show, since one true wife is better.
Declining both the vineyard and its profits, on Calmet's paraphrase, the speaker being content with his own and unwilling to trade his beloved for the riches of the universe.
Presenting a request to her royal husband, with her brothers in mind.
Asserting Christ's title to the church, which is better than Solomon's to his vineyard because it was purchased with blood.

outliers.note: Calls the passage about the wall and the door one of the strongest arguments for reading the book as a celebration of chaste wedded love, and dismisses an attempt to explain the palace of silver from a Druse head ornament shaped like a horn.
Turns the scene into a picture of domestic counsel, yoke-fellows who having laid their hearts together now lay their heads together to consider a sister and an estate.

themes: We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts: what shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for?
If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she be a door, we will inclose her with boards of cedar.
I am a wall, and my breasts like towers: then was I in his eyes as one that found favour.
Solomon had a vineyard at Baal–hamon; he let out the vineyard unto keepers; every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver.
My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred.

13.pericope_label: Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it... Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports one scholar's view that the closing words send the man away, though not harshly since she still calls him her beloved, and another's that the exchange is bantering coquetry, and settles it by refusing the imaginary shepherd some readers introduce into the scene against the text's own address to Solomon: to ignore a husband's request would be scornful, as singing unasked would be unseemly. Ellicott makes the thirteenth verse a reminiscence of courtship, when the lover envied everyone near the girl, and hears in the last verse the answer finally given to his sighing.

Gill observes that the Hebrew participle is feminine and so addresses the woman, records that the Greek made it masculine and that Ambrose accordingly had the church speaking to Christ while two other translators took it the other way, and refers the haste to the incarnation, to Christ's presence among his people, or to the first spread of the gospel.

Clarke takes the verse for a bridegroom asking leave to withdraw early in the morning, admits nobody can identify the mountains of spices beyond their being named for the trees that grew there, marks the end of the seventh night of the marriage week, and closes by stating that throughout his notes he has carefully avoided every attempt to spiritualize the song; Wesley makes the gardens the many congregations and the requested voice the church's prayer, praise and preaching.

Henry builds a parting scene, the spouse staying below in the gardens where she has work while Christ removes to the mountains of spices to act as her advocate, and draws from it the duty of Christ's friends to keep a good correspondence with one another.

debates.question: Who speaks in the thirteenth verse?

positions.view: Christ to the church; the Hebrew participle is feminine, though the Greek made it masculine and one Latin father accordingly reversed the speakers.
The bridegroom asking his wife's leave to withdraw in the morning, with the companions waiting to hear.
The lover in an earlier season, envying the companions who could see and hear her.

debates.question: What does the closing request mean?

positions.view: Permission to depart, with a plea for a quick return, closing the seventh night of the marriage week.
The answer at last given to the lover's sighs, compressing the wooing and wedding into two short verses.
Not a dismissal in any harsh sense; the alternative readings of coquetry and of an imaginary shepherd are both to be refused.
A prayer that Christ finish his work in the world quickly and take the church to himself.

outliers.note: Ends his commentary on the book with an explicit statement of method: he calls it the oldest pastoral in the world and beyond controversy the finest for imagery and colouring that ever came from a human pen, and declares that throughout his notes he has carefully avoided all attempts to spiritualize it.

Records that the Septuagint rendered the participle in the masculine, so that Ambrose read the verse as the church addressing Christ, while Symmachus and Aquila took it as Christ addressing the church.

themes: Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it.
Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices.
